entities.reviewNotes: Modern American cryptid (first reported 1966). Guardrail D-111: never reference the 1967 bridge collapse, bridges, or the real town. Omens only concern in-game events.
sources: Keel, John A. The Mothman Prophecies. Saturday Review Press, 1975.
Sergent, Donnie Jr. & Wamsley, Jeff. Mothman: The Facts Behind the Legend. Mothman Lives Publishing, 2001 (some listings give 2002).

entities.reviewNotes: Slavic folklore witch in a hut on chicken legs; ambiguous figure who tests visitors and rewards the polite and capable. Formidable and unimpressed; she judges, the leader is judged. Plain standard English: no accent, no dropped articles. Say 'Slavic', never a country; no food, drink, faith or politics jokes. 'Grandmother' is the tales' polite address; keep it sincere. Menace is fairy-tale, one clause, off screen, aimed at the leader or unnamed fairy-tale royalty. Never children, never followers, never detail.
sources: Johns, Andreas. Baba Yaga: The Ambiguous Mother and Witch of the Russian Folktale. International Folkloristics 3. New York: Peter Lang, 2004.
Afanas'ev, Aleksandr. Russian Fairy Tales. Trans. Norbert Guterman, commentary by Roman Jakobson. New York: Pantheon, 1945.

entities.reviewNotes: American folklore creature of the New Jersey Pine Barrens (winged, hooved, horse-headed). A loud, petty neighbour. No real people, living or historical. Never the Leeds name, the 'thirteenth child' birth story, real towns or dated sightings; 'the pines' only. Never mock Pine Barrens residents or use the word 'Piney'. Casual voice, no phonetic accent, no ethnic or mob stereotype. Mischief is property-level (fences, mailboxes, power); he never hurts people or animals.
sources: Regal, Brian & Esposito, Frank J. The Secret History of the Jersey Devil: How Quakers, Hucksters, and Benjamin Franklin Created a Monster. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2018.
McCloy, James F. & Miller, Ray Jr. The Jersey Devil. Wallingford, PA: Middle Atlantic Press, 1976.

entities.reviewNotes: Trickster spider of Akan (Ghana) folktales, carried to the Caribbean and the Americas; owner of all stories. Folktale figure only: clever, charming, a step ahead of the leader. Never call him a god. Never name or joke about the sky god or any Akan religious figure, rite or proverb. Standard English: no dialect or patois spelling, no 'Brer' forms. He wins by wit and bargains, never luck: no dice, cards or casino imagery. Foils are tale animals (Tiger, Snake) or the leader, never followers. No slavery or plantation jokes.
sources: Rattray, R. S. Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1930.
Marshall, Emily Zobel. Anansi's Journey: A Story of Jamaican Cultural Resistance. Kingston: University of the West Indies Press, 2012.

entities.reviewNotes: Original creation for this game (D-104): a vast, patient thing in deep water. Cosmic-horror in tone only. No names, places, quotations or stock phrases from any published mythos: never 'Deep One(s)', 'Old One(s)', 'Elder', invented-language chants or New England place names. Its hunger is for candles, flowers and attention; it never takes, eats or harms anyone. Sanity effects are comic only (D-112).
sources: Original to Cult Tycoon; see docs/DECISIONS.md D-104.
